tier_reason: The repo README carries the '15%x faster than perl5 overall, more than 2x faster then 5.14' sentence with no methodology; the project's own PerlBench page (perl11.github.io repo, cperl/bench-all/index.html, run 2019-06-14) gives per-build compilers and flags but no CPU model, and its numbers do not support the README claim, so first-party C with the claim corrected.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'about 15%x faster than perl5 overall, more than 2x faster then 5.14' and the least memory measured since 5.6; the STATUS page says 'about 20% faster than perl5 overall'. Neither links a measurement. The project's own PerlBench run (2019-06-14, 41 micro-tests, 5.6.2 = 100, higher is better) gives Average 142.9 for cperl 5.30.0c vs 134.8 for perl 5.30.0 (about 1.06x, derived from page data; cperl wins 26 of 41 tests) and 114.6 vs 102.6 at 5.22 (about 1.12x), but cperl is equal or slower at 5.24 (125.5 vs 127.0), 5.26 (132.4 vs 131.9) and 5.28 (134.7 vs 136.9). Against perl 5.14 (101.9) cperl 5.30 is about 1.40x, not 2x (derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: perl5 releases 5.6.2 to 5.30.0 on the same machine (PerlBench); the README names 'perl5' and 5.14
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Differs per side on the PerlBench page: cperl 5.28c/5.30c built with clang 7.0.1 -O3 -g -DLTO -flto=thin -msse4.2 -march=native; cperl 5.22c-5.26c with gcc 7.2.0/8.2.0/8.3.0 -O3 -g -msse4.2 -march=native; perl5 5.22-5.30 with gcc 8.3.0 -O2 -fwrapv and no -march; perl 5.14 with gcc 6.3.0 -O1 -g
corrections.hardware: Linux x86_64 machine ('reini'), Debian kernel 4.19.0-5-amd64; CPU model not stated
corrections.workload: PerlBench micro-benchmark suite (41 tests: arith, array, call, hash, loop, re, startup, string), scores relative to perl 5.6.2 = 100
corrections.caveats: The README's 15% (and the STATUS page's 20%) and '2x faster than 5.14' have no benchmark behind them; the project's own PerlBench page shows about 6% over perl 5.30.0 and cperl slower than or equal to perl5 at 5.24, 5.26 and 5.28. The comparison is confounded: cperl builds used -O3, -march=native and (5.28c/5.30c) clang thin LTO, while perl5 builds used gcc -O2 without -march, and the 5.14 baseline was built at -O1 -g. No CPU model. Archived read-only on 2023-06-01, last commit 2022-07-29; based on old perl5 releases, so it lags current perl5.

notes: Downgrade of the claim, not the tier: the 15%/20%/2x figures are unsupported and the project's own PerlBench run shows about 1.06x over perl 5.30.0 (cperl 5.30.0c) with cperl slower at 5.24 and 5.28, and with cperl built at -O3/-march=native/LTO against perl5 at -O2. perl5 is not one of the category baselines (CPython, Lua, MRI, V8); category language-interpreters is right. The cperl STATUS and bench-all pages are on blocked perl11.github.io but readable from the perl11/perl11.github.io repo via raw.githubusercontent.com.

tier_reason: First-party comparison repo by Expr's author with public go test code (expr_test.go, celgo_test.go, goja_test.go and the others, common.go) and Apple M2 stated, but no Go toolchain version, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchtime=20s; go.mod declares go 1.20, toolchain version not stated
corrections.workload: Evaluating one precompiled boolean expression per iteration, `(Origin == "MOW" || Country == "RU") && (Value >= 100 || Adults == 1)` over a 4-entry map, in each Go expression library (go test -bench, 20 s per benchmark), plus startsWith, custom function call and map(array of 100 ints, x*2) cases against cel-go only.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Main benchmark: expr 70.27 ns/op vs cel-go 91.27, goja 146.2, govaluate 152.9, otto 380.1, gval 412.9, evalfilter 990.6, bexpr 1276, starlark 2653 ns/op (expr about 1.3x faster than cel-go, derived from page data). Extra cases vs cel-go: startsWith 124.9 vs 134.8 ns/op, custom function 92.33 vs 110.2 ns/op, map predicate 4695 vs 24421 ns/op (about 5.2x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The comparison repo is written by Expr's own author; its README results were last updated with the 2023-08-14 'Update deps' commit, and go.mod pins github.com/antonmedv/expr v1.13.0 (Expr has since moved to expr-lang/expr), cel-go v0.17.1, goja 2023-08-12 and starlark-go 2023-08-14, so all versions are dated. One tiny precompiled expression per iteration says little about larger programs. The category baselines (CPython, Lua, MRI, V8) are not involved; goja and otto stand in for JavaScript engines and are Go-hosted. The Expr README itself only links to the comparison.

notes: Numbers match the comparison README exactly; the harness is fair on inspection (each library compiles outside the timed loop and the result is checked after it). Expr is an embeddable Go expression language rather than a general interpreter, so embedded-scripting (wave 12) may fit better than language-interpreters; no earlier-wave category applies.

tier_reason: First-party doc with public scripts and raw timing logs (info/scripts/sum2.sh, stat_2.sh, select.sh, filter.sh, groupby.sh, complex_sum.sh with .out and .out.mac files), a named Linux CPU (Xeon E5-2620 v4) and frawk build features, but no rustc/LLVM version (and the Mac CPU is only '8-core i9 2.3GHz'), so C by the compiler-version precedent; close to A.

corrections.baseline: gawk 5.1 (Linux) / 5.0.1 (macOS) run with -b, and mawk 1.3.4; one ad-hoc task also against a CPython csv-module script and a Rust csv-crate program (Python version not stated); xsv 0.13.0 and tsv-utils 2.1.1 also compared
corrections.claimed_speedup: Sum two columns, macOS: all_train TSV gawk 10.4 s and mawk 10.8 s vs frawk (LLVM) 3.1 s and parallel frawk 1.7 s; TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV gawk 14.0 s, mawk 42.0 s vs frawk 10.0 s / parallel 3.4 s. Linux: gawk 23.1 s vs frawk 14.7 s on TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV. Statistics (TREE_GRM_ESTN, macOS): gawk 1m13.3s and mawk 1m12.6s vs frawk (LLVM) 12.5 s TSV (about 5.9x vs gawk, derived from page data). Ad-hoc filtered weighted sum on CSV, macOS: CPython csv script 2m48.7s vs frawk (LLVM) 19.6 s (about 8.6x, derived from page data) and 4.9 s parallel; a quick Rust csv-crate program took 25.9 s. On a per-core basis frawk beats mawk and gawk but is slower than tsv-utils wherever tsv-utils ran. Group By Key is a tie with gawk (14.8 s vs 14.8 s on macOS; 22.1 s vs 23.5 s on Linux).
corrections.caveats: Author's own benchmarks; scripts and raw logs are in info/scripts but rustc/LLVM versions are missing and the numbers date from about 2021 (macOS Big Sur 11.2.1). frawk ties gawk on Group By Key, the Cranelift build is slower than gawk there on macOS, and frawk is slower than tsv-utils per core on every task tsv-utils ran; parallel select/filter does not preserve row order. The CPython comparison is one ad-hoc script, Python version unstated, and frawk's time includes its own compile. The doc asks readers to draw only modest conclusions. gawk and mawk are AWK implementations, not listed category baselines. Building needs nightly Rust by default and LLVM 12 for the LLVM backend; the maintainer noted in 2024 that he has much less time for bug fixes.

notes: All claimed numbers match info/performance.md and the sum2.sh.out.mac log (e.g. gawk 14.231 s, mawk 42.108 s); the page also compares against a CPython script, so baseline_in_list set true. frawk is an AWK implementation benchmarked on CSV/TSV against gawk, mawk, xsv and tsv-utils, so its real category is arguably csv-tabular (wave 3, parsing-and-text) rather than language-interpreters. Metadata checked: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 1.3k stars, last commit 2025-09-26 (stale), not archived.
